content:
We recently ran an experiment to try and replicate Anthropic's Claude C compiler but asking the agents to verify and prove the correctness of their generated code in Lean. Ultimately the agents were able to make progress on the implementation but utterly failed and got stuck on writing the proofs.

blog post: https://www.basis.ai/blog/verified-compiler/
github: https://github.com/BasisResearch/VerifiedJS

I am surprised that you write things like " The gap between stating a theorem and proving it remains beyond what current agents can do autonomously". This is an extremely general statement and arguably has been falsified by other people.

Isn't the conclusion rather that _you_ couldn't make the agents do your specific challenge? Or maybe you didn't use enough agents or weren't good enough at getting them to coordinate? Did you see that Meta were using 13000 agents together when they autoformalised 500 pages of a textbook? Maybe there are tricks you don't know about getting agents to collaborate? Of course formalising a textbook is arguably easier than doing what you were doing because the answers to everything are in the text.

I think you have raised an excellent challenge. Do you have an estimate for when it will be solved? Do you think that there's a chance that someone with $100K to spend on the challenge and the right knowhow could do it with today's technology within a week?
@Kevin Buzzard : Software verification is IME far more challenging than math

We are talking about replicating something on the scale of CakeML or sel4. Although compiler verification is a well explored verification challenge with theorems looking like “program semantics refines program semantics” at a very high level, the semantics for languages like JavaScript are highly non trivial to write because of the size of their specifications. Ecmascript 2025 is 847 pages of dense technical details. The wasm standard is another 300 pages.

My experience with agents (on a smaller scale) matches this article. They are very good at writing math proofs.
But when it comes to large proofs with heavy case distinctions, lean itself tends to gets slow and ai agents tend to lose track of relevant information.
https://github.com/manuelpuebla/amo-lean

Bas Spitters said:

https://github.com/manuelpuebla/amo-lean

Is this a good point of comparison though? There seem to be enough established formal verification pipelines and specifications for cryptology

I just meant that LLM supported compiler verification is possible. I have a couple of such projects myself. It's just not fully automatic (still requires pair programming), which seems to have been the goal from the experiment above.

Bas Spitters said:

I just meant that LLM supported compiler verification is possible. I have a couple of such projects myself. It's just not fully automatic (still requires pair programming), which seems to have been the goal from the experiment above.

Right~ I certainly don't want to dispute the claim that LLMs are useful for writing verified software, including writing compilers! I totally agree with that. I think the aspect that the blog post and experiment were investigating was the wider question of can agents use formal verification to raise the quality of their software.

Currently, I don't think we have a very clear idea of what the limits of fully autonomous agent-based workflows are. Clearly they are capable of somewhat impressive feats, such as writing a C compiler or stringing together components to produce a web browser, but those efforts are uncontroversially slop and unmaintainable (no one is claiming otherwise), but how far are we from agents just creating and running software entirely on their own? Does verification help bring us closer to that gap?

I think this negative result is fairly useful, and the challenge is something I'm happy to stand behind, because it a) helps orient people on what is and isn't possible and b) if someone completes it, there's a serious amount of non-trivial compiler theory that would have to be built to support it, that I think even the by-products would be useful to humanity (things like how to compile and prove async/await, prototypical inheritance, etc.). I've had varying degrees of responses to mentioning this result: some people have responded saying that of course, this is to be expected, no way agents could do something like this autonomously, and some people have been incredibly surprised I have found a task that didn't fall within a couple of weeks.

Fwiw, I had a similar but much smaller experiment from January which was trying to prove a textbook theorem entirely with vibe coding (I had to challenge myself to not be tempted to touch the code directly as much as possible). https://github.com/Shreyas4991/Vibe-Code-Experiment-Consensus

Back then codex was using GPT 5.2 and did not compress its context window

Full disclosure : This was the first time I used AI in code.
I think this experiment shows a stupendous improvement over mine.

Kevin Buzzard said:

I am surprised that you write things like " The gap between stating a theorem and proving it remains beyond what current agents can do autonomously". This is an extremely general statement and arguably has been falsified by other people.

Isn't the conclusion rather that _you_ couldn't make the agents do your specific challenge? Or maybe you didn't use enough agents or weren't good enough at getting them to coordinate? Did you see that Meta were using 13000 agents together when they autoformalised 500 pages of a textbook? Maybe there are tricks you don't know about getting agents to collaborate? Of course formalising a textbook is arguably easier than doing what you were doing because the answers to everything are in the text.

My belief is that this is fundamentally a task that is beyond the capabilities of agents at the current moment. As I said to Bas, I am happy to stand behind that claim because of the two reasons before, a) clearly there's no consensus on what agents are capable of doing, and as a verification researcher, my experience trying to use agents to do this, I am seeing them run into very basic walls and struggle to scale that leads me to that conclusion, so I do believe this (will elucidate more below), and b) if someone were to throw $100k at the problem and succeed, then this would be a valuable outcome in itself, because it would require in itself a large about of verification theory to handle the warts of JS' language design which would be of benefit to humanity in itself.

I'd conjecture that one aspect that makes software verification more difficult is that, unlike mathematics, software and software proofs are not driven by some notion of beauty or elegance, software and its verification obligations are a consequence of the arbitrary decisions of humans. Equality in javascript is not an equivalence relation. This is obviously a terrible idea. Yet still a compiler can not complain and must convolute itself to meet the whims of its language designers. The entirety of the language is filled with such arbitrary decisions, each of which require developing large and non-trivial amounts and fields of compiler verification theory to support.

The Meta and autoformalisation work is impressive, but in some sense it's an easier task, because the agents have a ground truth to work upon. In the case of a verified JS to WASM compiler, while the compilation implementation itself has a straightforward design (standard series of compiler passes, the agent was able to one-shot it), an appropriate proof strategy to prove correctness is unknown, different agents can have different choices for how features are encoded. and so there is inherently a consensus problem here that the agents are working around. I have a blog post about this here: https://kirancodes.me/posts/log-distributed-llms.html

I think you have raised an excellent challenge. Do you have an estimate for when it will be solved? Do you think that there's a chance that someone with $100K to spend on the challenge and the right knowhow could do it with today's technology within a week?

Again, I do not know when it will be solved. I hope it will be solved soon, because it will be a non-trivial achievement and require agents to autonomously do serious verification research that historically has taken several person-years of really smart PhD students to make any progress on. I don't think there's a chance that someone could just throw money at the problem. I guess the point of throwing 4 agents, and letting them run non-stop for 2 weeks was my attempt at throwing some money at the problem, and overall they just failed to make any progress.

To add to the above
@Kevin : here's a helpful analogy I developed to understand why PL and software verification is so much harder than math formalization. In mathematical (real/complex/harmonic) analysis, one deals with analysing classes of "nice" functions over various domains that are "nice". PL theory essentially vastly generalizes this to functions expressed as programs, and then to procedures. Compiler proofs are mathematical analysis applied to actual and messy programming language specs which are much much messier than even the ideal models of programs and procedures we use. They carry more and more information that needs to be included in your analysis.

Thanks for these clarifying comments. I think the thing that really hit home for me was Kiran's

Equality in javascript is not an equivalence relation. This is obviously a terrible idea. Yet still a compiler can not complain and must convolute itself to meet the whims of its language designers.

I totally agree that formalizing real mathematical proofs and formalizing proof of correctness of real programs are two very difficult problema. Despite being formally "the same thing", they seem to be located at very different places within the "make a term of this type" space.

The reason I think Kiran's challenge is an important one is that I would say that we now seem to have a very good understanding of what is and isn't possible in the autoformalization of mathematics, and it is possible to get a feeling for what is going to be possible because there are several groups working in this space and constantly spewing out datapoints. I find it quite surprising that the same is not happening (or at least I'm not noticing it happening) in proofs of program correctness; arguably this is a more important area. AI companies are looking for challenges and I hope that yours gets some traction Kiran.

I think another area where program verification differs from formalized math is that the theorems, definitions, and proofs often evolve in sync during the process of creating a verified program. Frequently one finds that a theorem statement needs to be generalized for induction, that a definition does not quite satisfy the desired properties, etc. Resolving this can be subtle: sometimes a definition is wrong, sometimes the theorem statement is too strong or weak, sometimes the proof strategy must be changed, etc. My understanding is that in formalized math, the theorem statements and definitions are much more fixed (but I don't have much experience in formalized math, so feel free to correct me if I am wrong). My smaller-scale (and much more interactive) experiences with using LLMs for software verification align with this experiment. One key difficulty I have found is in managing the tension between the fact that theorem statements and definitions must change throughout the process but the LLM left alone tends to weaken theorems and prove more trivial properties.

One thing I wish to point out is that at least since February, LLMs have gotten reasonably good at formalizing a mathematical proof when you can explain the proof structure you want, or interrupt them with a tip like "you know you are suffering from a weak IH, have you tried generalizing this variable" or "you are missing this typeclass instance from mathlib"

Of course this only works if you already know what the proof looks like more or less and you can debug Lean code reasonably quickly. As soon as you have multiple agents producing ginormous amounts of code in a short time, things are different.
(deleted)

The biggest difference in my mind is that there is not an equivalent to Mathlib for computer science, which seems to be an important component in how current AI generates proofs in Lean. And despite the fact the I am associated with CSLib which aspires to start filling this gap, as I've said before I think it is a reasonable question to ask if qualitative differences between CS and math formalization allow this to be a coherent goal. I'm really not sure! The beginning of Mathlib predates me, but I've seen you discuss before analogous skepticism in earlier days. I think we're at a similar point here, where it's not clear what is missing infrastructure versus inherent difficulty.

Yes at the beginning of mathlib, "formalize a theorem which I personally would find interesting" (an analogue of "formalize correctness of an actually useful program") was a fantasy and early adopters such as Kim, Patrick, Johan and myself quickly settled upon the far less ambitious (and hence actually feasible) "formalize an undergraduate degree" which it turned out had never been done before in a coherent manner. When this was basically achieved it was possible to do a few sporadic examples of "formalize a theorem which I find interesting" (and such things were done, often as publicity stunts) but the main part of the mathlib work switched to "formalize early graduate level mathematics from the standard textbooks" and I personally had no idea that making a robust library of this form would be such an important tool because autoformalization was going to become a reality.

I think one sociological difference between mathlib and cslib is that "formalize an undergraduate degree" was definitely in scope but had never been done before, whereas my impression is that there is a ton of cslib-style repos out there in plenty of other formal languages. One objection there was to mathlib at the time was "what is the point of just ploughing through an undergraduate degree, how will that lead to publications?". The trick was to convince enough people that it was worth doing anyway -- and of course the vast majority of mathlib is not linked to any publication. Another thing perhaps worth flagging was that (beyond the undergraduate todo page) there were never any concrete goals for mathlib (and indeed there is still no official statement from the maintainers about what is and isn't in scope). People were attracted to the undergraduate project because we had a big list of material which a generic mathematics undergraduate would typically understand and feel competent to have a go at. Perhaps cslib should have a big list of accessible goals with a maintainer who has a vision for how each goal should be formalized?

CSLib CONTRIBUTING.md (relatively new, cslib#358)

The foundational defintions content includes concepts already present in mathlib or concepts which should be in mathlib like graphs. Also the track A part of the pillar 1 section is heavily focussed on graph algorithms to the exclusion of several important topics which are equally foundational in TCS. Notably complexity theory is completely missing.
At least the algorithms and complexity part of this document needs substantial revisions

[...] People were attracted to the undergraduate project because we had a big list of material which a generic mathematics undergraduate would typically understand and feel competent to have a go at.[...]

I have the [citationless] impression that the "core curriculum" for CS has significantly less convergence than for undergraduate maths.
It's all so young! Owicki-Gries and Hindley-Milner were mid-70's, Lamport's vector clocks shortly after. Smyth and Plotkin's categorical "domain" fixpoints were in the 80's, likewise Liskov's behavioural subtyping, and AFAICT a lot of the canon on bisimulations and (co-/)simulations dates to the 90s. Arguably many of these can and ought be packaged as undergraduate material, but it feels to me like the canon — and pedagogy — diverges very quickly [EDIT: as measured by eg # semesters]

Yes the worlds of "undergraduate CS" and "undergraduate math" couldn't be more different. Undergraduate math seems to have basically stabilised and the main goal seems to be "get to the 1940s in some areas" whereas two of my kids just sat through undergrad CS degrees recently and they were learning stuff which didn't exist when I was an undergrad.

On the other hand, I think we could easily identify a couple of books that a large number of people would consider as great classics that were good foundations some decades ago and still are still great foundations today. Not all of CS undegrad is theory, so the Lean formalize part will be smaller than math undergraduate part, but I don't think we need to assume that it is fluid beyond us being able to agree on. Here's an example, purposely focusing on things whose editions came out a while ago:

* Introduction to Algorithms
* Elements of the Theory of Computation (first edition is better), https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/549820
* The formal semantics of programming languages,
* Is everything in Rosen's 1000 page textbook covered by mathlib (maybe it needs to be merely instantiated from mathlib theorems to be usable by mortal computer scientists)
